newsitem.title: USA: Texas separatist leader defies federal government.
newsitem.headline: Texas separatist leader defies federal government.

text.p: Richard McLaren, the leader of an armed separatist group caught in a standoff with police in west Texas, has pledged to die fighting rather than give up his campaign for an independent Lone Star nation.

An arrest warrant was issued against McLaren last December but the self-styled ambassador of the Republic of Texas separatist group has repeatedly challenged police to go in and haul him out of his remote mountain stronghold.
"If they try to come in here they'll suffer the consequences," McLaren told Reuters recently. "I'll die on my feet but never on my knees."

FBI agents and local and state police remained camped outside Mclaren's remote mountain compound on Monday, weighing whether to move against him, negotiate or withdraw. McLaren's main demand is that Texans be allowed to vote in a referendum on independence. He says he is confident a majority would vote in favour of the proposal.

The separatists grabbed two neighbours as hostages on Sunday and, after 12 tense hours, cut a late-night deal to release them in exchange for the return of McLaren's chief of security, who had been arrested earlier on weapons charges.

It was not clear how many supporters McLaren had inside the compound or how heavily armed his security forces were. He has talked repeatedly of martyrdom but also says the Republic's so-called defence forces and allied militias would strike back against any police raid.

"Within hours we'd have thousands of people here defending the embassy and spreading out across Texas," he said. There was no sign of any such response Sunday and state officials claim McLaren has an exaggerated view of his own power.

A balding, lanky man with clumps of wiry gray hair, McLaren looks more like an eccentric intellectual than an independence hero and is actually from Missouri, not Texas. He became the group's leader during an internal power struggle last year and stepped up the political and financial war on the federal government.

While he and other leaders claim they form a provisional government rather than a militia, they share much of the rhetoric of the far-right militia movement, which believes the United Nations is trampling on independent nations in its bid to set up a "new world order".

They established their own court system and issued a $93 trillion lien against the U.S. government, the United Nations and the Roman Catholic Church for allegedly plundering Texas' wealth. And McLaren pushed the strategy of tying up federal government agencies and Texas courts by filing liens on the property of public figures and private citizens.
The group also issued an estimated $3 million in false checks made out in the name of the Republic of Texas.

It was those alleged crimes and his refusal to attend a court hearing that led to an arrest warrant being issued against McLaren in December. But he insists the liens are legal and the checks are backed by the "full faith and credit" of the citizens of Texas.

Some former allies in the Republic of Texas have turned against McLaren in recent months and a rival faction claims he has been expelled from the group. At least two factions claim to be the provisional government of the Republic of Texas.
